title: What a test hands back
prompt:
Systolic pressures in eight patients on a drug, and eight on placebo:

```r
drug    <- c(128, 134, 121, 139, 125, 131, 127, 136)
placebo <- c(142, 138, 149, 135, 144, 151, 140, 146)
result  <- t.test(drug, placebo)
result
```

Printing `result` shows this:

```
       Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  drug and placebo
t = -4.5272, df = 13.874, p-value = 0.0004844
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -19.164014  -6.835986
sample estimates:
mean of x mean of y
  130.125   143.125
```

What is `result`, underneath that printout?
hint:
The printout looks like a report. But you stored it with `<-`, and later
exercises will pull single numbers back out of it.

options.text: A collection of named pieces — the p-value, the interval, the means — that you can take out one at a time
options.feedback:
Right. What you see printed is a tidy report, laid out for humans. The
output itself is a *list*: a set of named pieces, each of which you can
pull out on its own.

That matters because code rarely wants the whole report. It wants one
number — the p-value for a table, the interval for a figure — and
taking it from the list is far safer than copying it off the screen.

options.text: A block of text — the report you see
options.feedback:
It prints as text, but that's just how R chooses to show it. Underneath
are separate named pieces you can take out one by one, which you
couldn't do with a block of text.

The p-value is in there, but so is a lot else: the interval, the two
means, the name of the test. `result` holds all of it.

Close in spirit — it holds several things under names — but a data
frame needs every column to be the same length. These pieces aren't:
the p-value is one number, the interval is two. That's what a list
allows.

title: What's inside?
prompt:
`names()` lists the names of the pieces inside something. Use it on
`result`.
hint: The function name goes directly before the brackets.

solution.why:
Ten pieces, each with a name. Some you'll recognise from the printout —
`p.value`, `conf.int`, `estimate`, `method`. Others, like `stderr` and
`null.value`, are there even though the printout never showed them.

When you're handed a result you don't recognise, `names()` is the
quickest way to find out what's in it.

checks.on_fail: That didn't list the pieces inside `result`.

misconceptions.feedback:
`result$names` looks for a piece *called* `names` inside the list, and
there isn't one — so it quietly gives back nothing. `names()` is a
function: it goes in front, with `result` inside the brackets.

title: Taking out the p-value
prompt:
`$` takes one piece out of a list, just as it took one column out of a
data frame. Get the p-value.
hint: Use the name exactly as `names()` showed it.

solution.why:
`0.0004844103` — more digits than the printout showed, because the
printout rounds for display. The number in the list is the real one
that was stored.

You'll also see this written `result[["p.value"]]`, with double square
brackets. It does exactly the same thing.

misconceptions.feedback:
That works — but only by luck. When a name is cut short, `$` on a list
quietly fills in the rest, *if* only one name starts that way.
`p.val` can only mean `p.value`, so R gives you that.

It's fragile. It's also why `result$p` gives `NULL`: `p` could mean
`p.value` *or* `parameter`, so R won't guess. Always write the full
name.

You got `NULL` — nothing — and no error. `$` with a name that isn't in
the list quietly gives back nothing, the same as a misspelt column
name. The name is `p.value`, with a full stop, exactly as `names()`
printed it.

title: Which test did R run?
prompt:
You asked for a t-test. There's more than one kind. Click the part of the
printout that tells you which kind R actually ran.
hint: It's the line at the very top.

options.feedback:
Right — a *Welch* test. There are two common versions of this t-test.
Student's version assumes both groups are about equally spread out;
Welch's doesn't assume that, which makes it the safer choice when
you're not sure.

You never asked for Welch. It's the default: `t.test()`'s usage line
includes `var.equal = FALSE` — the groups' spread is *not* assumed to
be equal — and that picks Welch's version.

Welch is usually a sensible choice. But it's a decision made for you,
and it's worth knowing it was made. If a paper's methods say
"Student's t-test" and the code ran Welch, the numbers won't match.

This line tells you which data went into the t-test — here, the `drug`
and `placebo` vectors — but not which kind of test was run on them.

This is the result, not the method. The kind of test is named above
everything else.

title: Which mean is which?
prompt:
The printout ends with:

```
mean of x mean of y
  130.125   143.125
```

The code was `t.test(drug, placebo)`. Which group had the mean of 130.125?
hint:
`x` and `y` aren't names from your data. They're the names of
`t.test()`'s first two arguments.

options.feedback:
Right. `t.test()`'s first two arguments are called `x` and `y`, and
`drug` was written first — so it's `x`. The printout uses the
argument names, not your names.

Swap the order to `t.test(placebo, drug)` and the labels swap too,
along with the sign of the difference and the interval. Nothing warns
you. The order you wrote them in is the only record of which is which.

`x` is the first argument, and `drug` was written first. So `mean of
x` is the drug group — 130.125 — and placebo is `y`.

options.text: You can't tell from the output
options.feedback:
You can't tell from the output *alone* — which is exactly the trap. But
you can from the call: `x` is the first argument, and `drug` came
first.

title: One end of the interval
prompt:
The pieces of a list don't have to be the same size. The p-value is one
number; the confidence interval is two — a lower end and an upper end.

Get just the lower end of the confidence interval.
hint:
`result$conf.int` gives you both numbers, as a vector. You picked one value
out of a vector by position in module 5.

solution.why:
`$` takes the interval out of the list, and `[1]` takes the first number
out of the interval — one step, then another, read left to right.

If you print `result$conf.int` on its own, you'll also see a line
starting `attr(,"conf.level")`. That's a label attached to the numbers,
recording that this is a 95% interval. It isn't a third value, and you
can ignore it.

checks.on_fail: That isn't the lower end of the interval yet.

misconceptions.feedback:
That's both ends of the interval. Pick out the first one by position,
the way you picked values out of a vector.

title: Rounding a small p-value
prompt:
The p-value is `0.0004844103`. Rounding it for a table:

```r
round(result$p.value, 4)
```

R prints `5e-04`. What does that mean?
hint: The `e` means *times ten to the power of*.

options.feedback:
Right. `5e-04` is scientific notation: 5 × 10⁻⁴, which is 0.0005.
Calculators and spreadsheets write very small and very large numbers
the same way. R switches to it when a number is small, and you'll see
it constantly — tiny p-values often print as something like
`2.2e-16`.

One more thing worth knowing. Round to three places instead, and
`round(result$p.value, 3)` gives `0`. A p-value is never actually zero,
so never report it that way: write *p* < 0.001.

The `e-04` shrinks it: it means × 10⁻⁴, so the 5 moves four places to
the right of the decimal point. It's 0.0005.

Reasonable guess, but here `e` isn't the constant 2.718. It means
*times ten to the power of*, so `5e-04` is 5 × 10⁻⁴ — 0.0005.

It's a number, written compactly. `5e-04` is 5 × 10⁻⁴, which is
0.0005.

title: A missing value, handled quietly
prompt:
One placebo reading is missing:

```r
placebo <- c(142, 138, NA, 135, 144, 151, 140, 146)
```

In module 6, `mean(placebo)` would give `NA`. What does
`t.test(drug, placebo)` do?
hint: Not every function treats a missing value the same way.

options.text: Quietly leaves the missing reading out, and runs on the other seven
options.feedback:
Right — and it doesn't say so. `mean()` refuses to guess and gives
`NA`; `t.test()` drops the missing value and carries on. Different
functions, different rules.

The only clues are in the printout, and only if you compare it with the
one from exercise 1. The placebo mean is now 142.29 instead of 143.125
— the average of seven readings, not eight — and `df` has dropped from
13.874 to 12.994, because there's less data. So when a result comes
from data that has missing values, check how many values the function
actually used.

That's what `mean()` does, and it's a reasonable guess. But `t.test()`
takes a different approach: it drops the missing reading and runs on
what's left — without telling you.

options.text: Stops with an error about the missing value
options.feedback:
No error. It drops the missing reading and runs on the other seven,
and nothing in the printout says it did.
